::: {.solutions}

Marks: **(M1)** method, **(A1)** accuracy, **(B1)** independent. Total **71**.

Two habits to check: on an **equation**, did every root get tested against the case that produced it (reject
out-of-branch roots)? On a **graph/region**, did they split at every **corner** (where a modulus argument is
$0$) before doing anything else?

---

# Section A — Equations & inequalities

## Question 1 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**(a) $x=\tfrac43,\ 6$; (b) $x=1$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 M1 A1)**

**(a)** $\lvert2x-5\rvert=x+1$ needs $x+1\ge0$. Case $2x-5=x+1\Rightarrow x=6$ (✓, $\lvert7\rvert=7$); case
$2x-5=-(x+1)\Rightarrow3x=4\Rightarrow x=\tfrac43$ (✓, $\lvert-\tfrac73\rvert=\tfrac73=x+1$). Both valid.

**(b)** $\lvert x-3\rvert=2x$ needs $2x\ge0$. Case $x-3=2x\Rightarrow x=-3$ (**reject**, $2x<0$); case
$-(x-3)=2x\Rightarrow x=1$ (✓). Only $x=1$.

*Always check the right-hand side is $\ge0$ and that each root satisfies the sign of its own case — that is
how $x=-3$ is thrown out in (b).*
:::

---

## Question 2 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**$x\le-3$ or $x\ge\tfrac12$, i.e. $(-\infty,-3]\cup[\tfrac12,\infty)$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 B1)**

Both sides are $\ge0$, so square: $(3x+2)^{2}\ge(x-4)^{2}\Rightarrow(3x+2)^{2}-(x-4)^{2}\ge0$. Factor as a
difference of squares:
$$\big[(3x+2)-(x-4)\big]\big[(3x+2)+(x-4)\big]=(2x+6)(4x-2)=4(x+3)(2x-1)\ge0,$$
so $(x+3)(2x-1)\ge0\Rightarrow x\le-3$ or $x\ge\tfrac12$.

*Squaring is legal because both sides are non-negative; factor as a difference of two squares rather than
expanding.*
:::

---

## Question 3 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**$-2$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 B1)**

$\lvert x^{2}-2x\rvert=\lvert x-2\rvert\Rightarrow x^{2}-2x=\pm(x-2)$.

- $x^{2}-2x=x-2\Rightarrow x^{2}-3x+2=0\Rightarrow(x-1)(x-2)=0\Rightarrow x=1,2$.
- $x^{2}-2x=-(x-2)\Rightarrow x^{2}-x-2=0\Rightarrow(x-2)(x+1)=0\Rightarrow x=2,-1$.

Distinct solutions $\{-1,1,2\}$; product $(-1)(1)(2)=-2$.

*$\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert\iff A=\pm B$ — no non-negativity condition needed. The root $x=2$ appears in
both branches but is counted once.*
:::

---

## Question 4 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**$k<4$: none; $k=4$: infinitely many (all $-3\le x\le1$); $k>4$: two.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 B1)**

$\lvert x+3\rvert+\lvert x-1\rvert$ is the total distance from $x$ to $-3$ and to $1$. Its **minimum** is the
gap between them, $\lvert1-(-3)\rvert=4$, achieved for **every** $x$ in $[-3,1]$ (a flat bottom); outside, it
rises with slope $2$. So a level $k$ meets it in **none** ($k<4$), **a whole segment** ($k=4$), or **two**
points ($k>4$).

*A sum of two distances is flat and equal to the gap between the two points, then V-shaped outside — that flat
bottom is why $k=4$ gives infinitely many solutions.*
:::

---

## Question 5 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**$\big(-\sqrt7,-1\big)\cup\big(1,\sqrt7\big)$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 B1)**

$\lvert x^{2}-4\rvert<3\Rightarrow-3<x^{2}-4<3\Rightarrow1<x^{2}<7\Rightarrow1<\lvert x\rvert<\sqrt7$. So
$x\in(-\sqrt7,-1)\cup(1,\sqrt7)$.

*Unfold to a double inequality on $x^{2}$, then take roots: $1<x^{2}<7$ becomes $1<\lvert x\rvert<\sqrt7$,
which is two symmetric intervals.*
:::

# Section B — Graphs, x|x| & regions

## Question 6 **[6]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**(a) roots $1,3$, dip flipped up to a local max $(2,1)$; (b) even, roots $\pm1,\pm3$, minima $(\pm2,-1)$,
local max $(0,3)$; (c) four.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 M1 A1 M1 A1)**

$f(x)=(x-1)(x-3)$ has minimum $(2,-1)$.

- **(a) $\lvert f\rvert$:** the part between the roots (below the axis) flips **up**, so the dip becomes a
  hump with a corner-free local max $(2,1)$; roots stay at $x=1,3$.
- **(b) $f(\lvert x\rvert)$:** keep $x\ge0$ and mirror in the $y$-axis — even, with roots $\pm1,\pm3$, minima
  $(\pm2,-1)$, and a local maximum $(0,3)$ at the join.
- **(c)** $\lvert f(x)\rvert=\tfrac12\Rightarrow f=\tfrac12$ or $f=-\tfrac12$. $f=\tfrac12$:
  $x^{2}-4x+\tfrac52=0\Rightarrow x=2\pm\tfrac{\sqrt6}2$ (two). $f=-\tfrac12$: $x^{2}-4x+\tfrac72=0
  \Rightarrow x=2\pm\tfrac{\sqrt2}2$ (two, since the discriminant $2>0$ and $f$ dips to $-1<-\tfrac12$). **Four**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-4,6,600); f=x**2-4*x+3
fig,ax=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(5.0,4.6))
ax[0].plot(x,np.abs(f),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2); ax[0].plot([1,3],[0,0],'o',color='crimson'); ax[0].plot(2,1,'o',color='crimson')
ax[0].set_title('y = |f(x)|: dip flipped up, local max (2,1)',fontsize=9)
ax[1].plot(x,(np.abs(x))**2-4*np.abs(x)+3,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
ax[1].plot([1,3,-1,-3],[0,0,0,0],'o',color='crimson'); ax[1].plot(0,3,'o',color='#2ca02c')
ax[1].set_title('y = f(|x|): even, minima (±2,−1), local max (0,3)',fontsize=9)
for a in ax: a.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.5); a.grid(alpha=0.2); a.set_ylim(-2,5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*In (c) count where the two horizontal levels $f=\pm\tfrac12$ cut the parabola; $f=-\tfrac12$ has solutions
only because $f$ reaches down to $-1$.*
:::

## Question 7 **[5]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**$x=1$ and $x=-1-\sqrt2$ — two solutions.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 A1 B1)**

Split at $x=0$.

- $x\ge0$: $x\lvert x\rvert=x^{2}$, so $x^{2}=2x-1\Rightarrow(x-1)^{2}=0\Rightarrow x=1$ (✓, a repeated root
  but one point).
- $x<0$: $x\lvert x\rvert=-x^{2}$, so $-x^{2}=2x-1\Rightarrow x^{2}+2x-1=0\Rightarrow x=-1\pm\sqrt2$. Only
  $x=-1-\sqrt2$ is $<0$; $x=-1+\sqrt2\approx0.41$ is rejected (wrong branch).

So two distinct solutions.

*On each branch $x\lvert x\rvert$ is an ordinary quadratic ($x^{2}$ or $-x^{2}$); keep only the roots lying in
the branch that produced them.*
:::

---

## Question 8 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**One: $x=1$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 B1)**

Corners at $x=-2,1$.

- $x\ge1$: $(x-1)+(x+2)=2x+1=3x\Rightarrow x=1$ (✓).
- $-2\le x<1$: $(1-x)+(x+2)=3=3x\Rightarrow x=1$ (not in $[-2,1)$ — reject).
- $x<-2$: $(1-x)+(-x-2)=-2x-1=3x\Rightarrow x=-\tfrac15$ (not $<-2$ — reject).

Only $x=1$.

*The left-hand side is $3$ on the flat middle and rises to the right; the line $3x$ overtakes it exactly at
$x=1$.*
:::

## Question 9 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**A diamond centred $(1,-2)$; area $18$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 B1)**

$\lvert x-1\rvert+\lvert y+2\rvert=3$ is a diamond (square rotated $45^\circ$) centred at $(1,-2)$ with
vertices $3$ units along each axis: $(4,-2),(-2,-2),(1,1),(1,-5)$. Its diagonals are both $2\times3=6$, so
area $=\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot6=18$ (equivalently $2\cdot3^{2}$).

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
V=[(4,-2),(1,1),(-2,-2),(1,-5),(4,-2)]
plt.figure(figsize=(3.6,3.2)); plt.plot([p[0] for p in V],[p[1] for p in V],'-o',color='#2b6cb0')
plt.plot(1,-2,'o',color='crimson'); plt.annotate('(1,−2)',(1,-2),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,2),fontsize=8)
plt.grid(alpha=0.3); plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.title('|x−1|+|y+2|=3: area 18',fontsize=9); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*For $\lvert x-h\rvert+\lvert y-k\rvert=r$ the area is $2r^{2}$; here $r=3$.*
:::

## Question 10 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**$64$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 B1)**

$\lvert2x\rvert+\lvert y\rvert\le8$ is a diamond with $x$-intercepts $\pm4$ (set $y=0$) and $y$-intercepts
$\pm8$ (set $x=0$). Its diagonals are $8$ (horizontal) and $16$ (vertical), so area
$=\tfrac12\cdot8\cdot16=64$.

*The coefficient on $x$ squashes that axis: $\lvert2x\rvert\le8$ reaches only to $x=\pm4$, half as far as the
$y$-axis.*
:::

# Section C — Integrals, distances & nesting

## Question 11 **[5]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**$\dfrac{49}{6}$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 A1 B1)**

$x^{2}-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)$ is negative on $(-1,2)$ and positive on $[-2,-1]$ and $[2,3]$. Split at the roots:
$$\int_{-2}^{-1}(x^{2}-x-2)\,\mathrm dx-\int_{-1}^{2}(x^{2}-x-2)\,\mathrm dx+\int_{2}^{3}(x^{2}-x-2)\,\mathrm dx
=\frac{11}{6}+\frac{9}{2}+\frac{11}{6}=\frac{49}{6}.$$

*The modulus forces a sign flip on the middle piece where the quadratic is negative; split at the roots
$-1,2$ before integrating.*
:::

---

## Question 12 **[5]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**$4$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 A1 B1)**

$\lvert x^{2}-1\rvert$ is **even**, so integrate over $[0,2]$ and double. On $[0,1]$, $x^{2}-1\le0$; on
$[1,2]$, $\ge0$:
$$2\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}(1-x^{2})\,\mathrm dx+\int_{1}^{2}(x^{2}-1)\,\mathrm dx\right]
=2\!\left[\tfrac23+\tfrac43\right]=2\cdot2=4.$$

*Even symmetry halves the work; then split the half-integral at the corner $x=1$ where $x^{2}-1$ changes
sign.*
:::

---

## Question 13 **[5]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**Least value $10$, at every $x\in[4,6]$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 A1 B1)**

Pair the points from the outside in. $\lvert x-1\rvert+\lvert x-9\rvert\ge9-1=8$, least on $[1,9]$; and
$\lvert x-4\rvert+\lvert x-6\rvert\ge6-4=2$, least on $[4,6]$. Both minima hold simultaneously on the overlap
$[4,6]$, giving total least value $8+2=10$.

*For an even number of points the sum of distances is minimised on the **middle interval** (here between the
two central points $4$ and $6$); add the paired gaps.*
:::

## Question 14 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**$18$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 B1)**

$y=\lvert x-2\rvert$ is a V with vertex $(2,0)$; $y=6-\lvert x-2\rvert$ is a $\Lambda$ with peak $(2,6)$. They
meet where $\lvert x-2\rvert=3$, i.e. $x=-1,5$ (both at $y=3$). The enclosed shape is a kite with horizontal
diagonal from $(-1,3)$ to $(5,3)$ of length $6$, and vertical diagonal from $(2,0)$ to $(2,6)$ of length $6$:
area $=\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot6=18$.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-3,7,400)
plt.figure(figsize=(4.6,3.0)); plt.plot(x,np.abs(x-2),color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y=|x−2|'); plt.plot(x,6-np.abs(x-2),color='#dd6b20',lw=2,label='y=6−|x−2|')
plt.plot([-1,5,2,2],[3,3,0,6],'o',color='crimson')
plt.legend(fontsize=8); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.title('kite: diagonals 6 and 6 → area 18',fontsize=9); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*Two V/Λ graphs enclose a kite; use $\tfrac12 d_1 d_2$ with the horizontal and vertical diagonals.*
:::

## Question 15 **[5]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**Four: $x=-2,\ 0,\ 4,\ 6$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 A1 B1)**

Peel the outer modulus: $\big\lvert\lvert x-2\rvert-3\big\rvert=1\Rightarrow\lvert x-2\rvert-3=\pm1$, so
$\lvert x-2\rvert=4$ or $\lvert x-2\rvert=2$.

- $\lvert x-2\rvert=4\Rightarrow x=6$ or $x=-2$.
- $\lvert x-2\rvert=2\Rightarrow x=4$ or $x=0$.

All four are valid (each $\lvert x-2\rvert$ value is $\ge0$). Four solutions.

*Work outwards: the outer $=1$ gives two inner values $4,2$, each a genuine modulus equation with two roots —
$2\times2=4$.*
:::

---

## Question 16 **[4]**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer
**(a) $\ge4$, equality iff $1\le x\le5$; (b) $1\le x\le5$.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1 A1 B1)**

**(a)** By the triangle inequality, $\lvert x-1\rvert+\lvert x-5\rvert=\lvert x-1\rvert+\lvert5-x\rvert\ge
\lvert(x-1)+(5-x)\rvert=\lvert4\rvert=4$. Equality holds when $x-1$ and $5-x$ have the **same sign** (or one is
zero), i.e. $1\le x\le5$.

**(b)** Hence $\lvert x-1\rvert+\lvert x-5\rvert=4$ exactly on the segment $1\le x\le5$.

*The sum equals the gap between the two points precisely on the interval between them — outside it, at least
one distance is "wasted" and the sum exceeds $4$.*
:::
